thesis.question: How should product teams plan when generative models are part of the product and keep changing?
thesis.claim: Model-powered product teams should plan recurring, evaluation-led reinterpretations of workflows around changing models while preserving a stable customer promise, because a new model can enable previously infeasible workflows while breaking behavior that an existing customer job depends on.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that model releases are chiefly component upgrades within a stable feature roadmap, so benchmark improvements justify adoption without reconsidering workflows and customer fit.
thesis.so_what: Roadmaps, discovery, briefs, and release decisions need explicit model assumptions and customer evidence so that repeated rebuilds protect value rather than follow novelty.
thesis.how_why: A model change can remove workflow constraints and introduce new failure modes at once; only comparison on real user jobs, controls, trust boundaries, cost, and business outcomes shows which changes deserve commitment.

supporting_claims.claim: A model used in the customer product changes product possibilities and assumptions in a way that a development assistant does not.
Externally changing models can regress local fit, so seasonal planning extends outcome-focused management rather than assuming monotonic upgrades.
Comparative evaluation and direct customer evidence determine whether a model-driven change creates product and business value.
A stable customer promise and trust boundary let teams reinterpret model-dependent workflows without losing product identity.
A repeatable scouting, specification, evaluation, and selective-release loop separates exploration from commitment and retains learning.

role.contribution: Extends the journal's outcome and evaluation discipline to products whose own behavior changes with the model material.

flow.rationale: First distinguish the product problem from faster delivery, then explain the fashion analogy, external model change, short seasons, and the addition to modern product management. Only then introduce the operating loop and its fad-driven failure, followed by evaluation infrastructure, customer evidence, and stable commitments. Team routines, principles, anti-patterns, and self-questions apply those criteria before the final synthesis and leadership hand-off. Putting the loop before the model-material distinction would resemble generic speed advice; putting the practical rules before evaluation and the stable promise would leave their decision criteria unexplained. Moving the questions before the close lets the essay finish by joining stable purpose to evaluated change.
